When the signals disagree · and which one to trust
Different gauges sometimes point opposite ways. That is normal. Here is each clash in plain words, with the side to lean on for now.
⚠ These two disagree: Crash Index 0/10: calm, no signal aligned vs VIX Spike Tier 3/4 HIGH: 69% probability, backwardation active
The Crash Index reads completed price damage; the VIX Spike detector reads what options traders are paying to hedge against what has not happened yet. They describe different time horizons. Backwardation (near-term volatility priced above long-dated volatility) is a structural positioning signal. Trust the VIX side: it is leading, not lagging.
⚠ These two disagree: Regime State score 8: STABLE, no regime shift detected vs Macro Regime: TRANSITIONAL at only 25% confidence
The regime-state model says no break has completed; the macro regime classifier says it cannot identify what environment you are in. A regime can be 'stable' in the sense that no shift has landed while simultaneously being 'transitional' in the sense that the old regime's structure is eroding. The **25%** confidence is the more actionable read: don't size for a clean, defined regime.

If that correlation holds above +0.70 while VIX backwardation persists and regime confidence stays at 25%, the surface calm is the setup for a repricing, not an all-clear.

Macro Regime — where are we structurally
AI read · macro regime

The macro regime is classified as TRANSITIONAL with a confidence of only 25%. That is the model saying it cannot place current conditions inside any established category with conviction.

The regime state score of 8 says no shift has completed, but the MIXED bias in the regime state tells you the signals pulling in opposite directions are roughly balanced. TRANSITIONAL periods with low regime confidence are where the biggest sizing errors happen: participants commit to the prior regime's playbook while the next one is already setting up.

With confidence at 25%, you hold what you own, reduce new risk, and wait for the macro regime read to firm above 50% before adding directional exposure in either direction.

Dow Theory generalized · cross-asset divergences
Cross-asset divergence radar — Cross-asset divergence watch
AI read · divergences in plain English

Divergence, in plain terms: two assets that have historically moved together start decoupling, and their relationship drifts away from the baseline that held for months. Correlation drift is the measure of how far that drift has gone.

The composite divergence zone is ELEVATED: 48.8% of all monitored asset pairs are diverging, with 19 showing a bearish bias versus only 2 bullish. Mother Jaws (the aggregate divergence composite) scores 100, its ceiling reading.

Six pairs each register a DEEP DIVERGENCE score of 80. The SPY-TLT drift from +0.12 to +0.74 is the most consequential: stocks and long-duration Treasury bonds, which typically move inversely, are now moving in the same direction.

That kills the classic multi-asset hedge. SMH vs SPY moved from +0.11 to +0.81, locking semiconductors and the broad market in step with no dispersion to trade inside the tech complex.

Copper vs gold drifted from +0.14 to +0.82: two assets that normally diverge along growth-versus-safety lines are now correlated. When unrelated asset classes compress into the same correlation simultaneously, a single macro driver is overriding individual fundamentals.

That driver has not yet shown up in spot price.

AI read · the cross-region tape

The KOSPI is the number that demands attention: +16.5% over five days, the largest five-day move of any major index in the cross-region scan, against an HSI that gained only +0.4% over the same period. The spread between Seoul and Hong Kong is the sharpest regional dispersion in the data and warrants a read on whether that move reflects a structural re-rating or a short-covering event, because the answer changes the Asian risk appetite signal heading into the US session.

In Europe, the STOXX 50 added +3.7% while the FTSE lost -0.2%: continental Europe outperforming UK, which carries more commodity-cycle exposure. In the US, NDX led at +4.5% while RUT trailed at +1.9%: large-cap growth over small-cap cyclicals, consistent with the quality-over-breadth pattern visible everywhere else.

Crypto had ETH at +3.1% ahead of SOL at +0.7%. The consistent signal across all four regions is the same: large-cap tech and quality international assets leading, small-caps, UK, and crypto alts lagging.

Crash Index — 10 lead-signal radar 1/10 · WATCH — 1-2 signals, monitoring
AI read · volatility & crash, reconciled

The Crash Index at 0 of 10 means not one signal in the crash-detection framework is aligned: no trend breakdown, no breadth collapse, no forced-selling marker visible in price. The VIX Spike detector sits at Tier 3 of 4, HIGH, with a 69% probability of a volatility spike, and backwardation is active.

These readings describe different markets on different time horizons. The Crash Index watches what has already happened in spot price.

The VIX Spike detector watches what options traders are paying to protect against what has not happened yet. Backwardation means near-term volatility costs more than long-dated volatility: buyers are paying a premium for protection right now, not deferring it.

That is defensive positioning, not complacency. This combination of calm spot prices and expensive near-term protection is what you see before a vol expansion lands, not after one.

Plain-English read · the Crash Index
Think of this as a smoke alarm, not a market forecast. Each of the 10 rows is a signal that led real crashes, checked over 15 years of S&P 500 history (Bonferroni-validated, so it survived a strict false-positive test). In a calm market it sits near zero by design — a low number is the alarm working, not a broken gauge. It only earns your attention when 3 or more rows light up together. Today it reads 1/10, so the tape is calm and there is no crash setup.

How to read
Each row = an independent signal Bonferroni-validated over 15 years of SPY. The structural (DXY, SKEW, MOVE) signal a regime change over 30-90 days. The stress (HYG/IEF, VIX3M/VIX, STLFSI4) ring at 5-30 days. The triggers (SPY -2% in 5d, VIX +30% in 3d) are short-term breakouts. For a tactical decision: 3+ signals simultaneously aligned = real probability of stress, never on isolated signal (framework rule).

Strict sizing: tier 2 = 1-2% book hedges, tier 3 = 3-5% long-vol, tier 4 = 5-10% MAX (rare confluence).

Reading the table — Z-Score: number of standard deviations vs rolling 100d mean. |Z| > 2 = Kerberos entry threshold, |Z| > 2.5 = extreme (best R/R on mean-reversion). %B: position within Bollinger Bands (1.0 = upper band, 0 = lower band).

Aggregate reading — the mean of Z-scores gives a global regime indicator. Positive → cross-asset overbought market (Risk-On, watch reversal). Negative → oversold (Risk-Off, possible bottoming).
How to read
Persist = number of consecutive days above |Z| > 2.0 (Kerberos threshold). Persist ≥ 3d = validated signal (the divergence has become a regime, not a spike). Persist 1-2d = to watch. Persist 0d = dead signal. Sort on this column to find established regimes worth trading.
Glossary — 18 terms to understand the dashboard
Z-Score
Number of standard deviations vs the historical mean (rolling 100 days). Z=0 = normal level · |Z|>2 = stress · |Z|>2.5 = extreme.
Bollinger Bands
Bands drawn at ±2.2σ around a 100-day moving average. When the price exits the bands = statistically extreme signal.
Backwardation
Inverted curve: immediate fear exceeds far fear (e.g. VIX > VIX3M). Short-term panic signal.
Contango
Normal situation where far fear exceeds immediate fear. Extreme contango = complacency.
Half-life
Number of days required for a gap to the mean to halve. Measures the speed of mean-reversion.
Cointegration
Two assets that move together in the long term despite short-term fluctuations. Statistical basis of pair-trading.
Mean-reversion
Strategy betting that a gap to the mean will close. Inverse of momentum (which bets on continuation).
Breadth
Width of participation in the rally. Good breadth = many stocks rising. Bad breadth = only a few mega-caps pull the index.
Hedge ratio
Quantity of asset B to short to neutralize 1 long unit of asset A. Calculated via OLS regression on historical returns.
Lead-time
Delay between a signal's appearance and the event it predicts. Structural = 30-90d · stress = 5-30d · triggers = 1-10d.
Bonferroni
Statistical correction for multiple testing. When testing 100 signals, some seem valid by chance. Bonferroni divides the significance threshold by the number of tests to eliminate these false positives.
MCPT (Monte Carlo Permutation Test)
Robustness test: data is randomly shuffled 5000-10000 times to see if the signal appears by chance. If p < 0.05, the signal is probably real.
Walk-forward
Test where the model is trained on the first years (e.g. 2010-2020) and tested on the following years (2020-2025). Avoids in-sample overfitting.
Tail-hedge
Hedge against an extreme crash (-20% or more). Bought via deeply out-of-the-money puts. SKEW measures institutional demand for this type of insurance.
Mega-caps
The 7-10 largest market caps in the SPX (AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, GOOGL, AMZN, META, TSLA). Weigh ~35% of the index.
Cap-weighted vs Equal-weighted
SPY = weighted by capitalization (mega-caps dominate). RSP = each stock weighs 0.2%. Comparing both reveals concentration.
Risk parity
Portfolio strategy that balances risk (not capital) across asset classes. Stressed when stocks/bonds correlations turn positive (inflation regime).
framework rule
Fundamental principle: a solo signal = noise, 3+ aligned signals = real edge. All panel signals are Bonferroni-validated over 15 years of SPY.
